analysis.one_liner: Conditions federal airport funding on airports paying service workers at least $15 an hour with benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 17 senators, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in March 2023 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required airports with small, medium, or large hubs to certify, as a condition of receiving federal airport project grants and passenger facility charge money, that their service workers earn at least the highest of $15 an hour, the applicable Service Contract Act prevailing wage, the federal contractor minimum wage, or the state or local minimum wage, plus comparable fringe benefits. Covered workers include security officers, baggage and ramp handlers, cleaners, wheelchair attendants, ticketing and check-in staff, and food, retail, and lounge workers, including those employed by contractors and subcontractors. It would also have applied the same conditions retroactively to airport grants and terminal money from the 2021 infrastructure law. The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage airport service workers gain the most: baggage handlers, cabin cleaners, wheelchair attendants, security officers, ticketing agents, and food and retail workers at nearly every commercial hub airport in the country, including workers hired through contractors and subcontractors. They would get a pay floor of at least $15 an hour (or the applicable prevailing wage if higher) plus fringe benefits, and workers in higher-cost or higher-wage classifications would get the Service Contract Act prevailing wage, which in many airports exceeds $15. Travelers also benefit indirectly, since the bill's stated aim is a better-paid, more stable workforce with less turnover in security-sensitive airport jobs.

how_it_helps.text: It sets a pay floor for covered airport service workers at the highest of $15 an hour, the local Service Contract Act prevailing wage, the federal contractor minimum wage, or the applicable state or local minimum wage.

It requires those workers to receive fringe benefits at least equal to Service Contract Act or state/local minimums, with the Labor Department issuing wage determinations for each worker classification within 90 days of enactment.

It applies to workers regardless of any subcontracting arrangement, so companies could not avoid the wage floor by shifting workers through layers of contractors, and it does not preempt state or local laws that set higher standards.

It would apply the standards retroactively to federal airport infrastructure grants and the Airport Terminal Program funded by the 2021 infrastructure law, conditioning money already appropriated on compliance.

analysis.who_pays: Airlines and the contractors that employ airport service workers would bear higher wage and benefits costs, and those costs would likely be passed partly to travelers through ticket, food, and retail prices. Airport operators would take on annual certification and compliance-reporting duties and would risk losing federal project grants, including infrastructure law money, if their on-site employers failed to certify compliance.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises labor costs for airlines, airport restaurants and shops, and security and cleaning contractors, and some of those costs would likely be passed on to travelers through higher concession prices or added fees.

Airports and their contractors would take on new certification and annual reporting duties, and an airport that failed to certify could lose federal project grants, including money already appropriated under the 2021 infrastructure law, which could delay terminal and runway improvements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: hundreds of thousands of airport service workers, many earning near minimum wage, would get a enforceable wage-and-benefits floor tied to the federal money their airports already receive, with no new spending. The main costs are higher labor bills for airlines, catering companies, and airport concession and security contractors, which could be passed into airfares and airport food prices, and added compliance paperwork for airport operators. The bill uses federal grant conditions rather than a direct mandate, so its strength depends on enforcement by the Transportation Department, and enforcement was left largely to the Secretary's discretion. It died without a hearing or a vote, so none of its benefits or costs were ever tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee in March 2023, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: S. 753 was introduced in the Senate on March 9, 2023 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no committee markup, no committee report, and no floor vote at any point during the 118th Congress.
Seventeen senators sponsored the bill, all Democrats or allied independents, including Majority Leader Chuck Schumer; no Republican signed on.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airline ground-handling, catering, and airport concession and security contractors keep paying their current wages, and airports keep access to federal infrastructure grants without any wage certification. Airline passengers' ticket and concession prices are unaffected.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airport contractors and airlines paying current wages

industries.industry: Airport service contractors (food service, retail, cleaning, security, ground handling)
industries.note: These companies would have to pay their airport workers at least $15 an hour or the applicable prevailing wage, plus fringe benefits, directly cutting into the low-wage labor model much of the industry runs on. The bill explicitly counts workers regardless of subcontracting arrangements, closing the usual route around wage rules.

Airlines use contractors for baggage handling, ramp work, catering, and passenger assistance; the bill would raise the cost of those services at every small, medium, and large hub airport. Airlines have historically opposed wage mandates for the contractor workers who handle their passengers and planes.

Airport sponsors would face annual certification and compliance-reporting duties and could lose federal project grants if their contractors underpay workers. In practice the requirement pushes the wage costs onto the contractors and airlines that employ the workers, while the airports' federal funding stays intact if they comply.
